THOUGHT: This 23-year-old male experienced sudden loss of consciousness (syncope) during intense physical exertion (pitching), with rapid return of consciousness after CPR—indicating a transient, severe disruption of cerebral perfusion. The absence of trauma, seizure history, metabolic derangements (normal electrolytes, glucose not listed but no diabetes history), and normal neurological exam makes primary neurological or metabolic causes unlikely. The cardiovascular examination reveals key red flags: prominent double apical impulse (suggestive of hypertrophied left ventricle), S4 gallop (indicative of stiff, noncompliant left ventricle with impaired ventricular filling), and prominent A wave in the JVP (reflecting increased right ventricular diastolic pressure due to impaired left ventricular relaxation/filling — often seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [HCM]). ECG shows possible left ventricular hypertrophy, and echocardiogram confirms asymmetric septal hypertrophy without valvular disease — the hallmark structural finding in HCM. Importantly, HCM is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, typically triggered by exertion due to dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction, ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., polymorphic VT or VF), or ischemia from mismatched myocardial oxygen supply/demand. Normal cardiac enzymes rule out acute myocardial infarction; absence of murmurs does not exclude HCM (murmurs may be absent at rest or in non-obstructive forms). Family history is negative, but ~60% of HCM cases are sporadic or de novo mutations; genetic testing would be indicated but is not required for clinical diagnosis. All findings converge on hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as the underlying substrate for exercise-induced sudden cardiac arrest.

DIAGNOSIS: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
